{"id": "56:73/q05", "question": "Who are “al-muqwīn” for whom fire is provision?", "turns_on": "The competing derivations invoke empty wilderness, empty dwellings, empty stomachs or provisions, poverty and wealth as opposites, or tending the fire; some extend the designation to every user of fire.", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q05/p1", "position": "People traveling or staying in barren, uninhabited country.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, al-Farrāʾ, al-Layth, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabarī and others derive the term from qawāʾ, desolate land, or an emptied house; al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabarī, al-Nābigha, ʿAntara and al-Samīn cite poetry for empty dwellings. Al-Ṭabarī prefers travelers without provisions from the empty-dwelling expression; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers barren-country usage as most idiomatic and says Ibn ʿAbbās's 'travelers' is close to it. Al-Ḥasan says travelers carry fire in cloths and bags. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabarī include desert dwellers, Bedouins or residents of barren land; Ibn Kathīr notes a derivation from qiy/qiwa, a distant barren place. Al-Biqāʿī says the designation can apply to someone suited to wilderness even elsewhere. Bursawī describes country without water, speech or buildings. Al-Ālūsī says aqwā parallels aṣḥara ('entered the desert'); al-Thaʿlabī calls this the majority view."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p2", "position": "Everyone who uses fire, whether resident or traveler.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and ʿIkrima explicitly include residents and travelers; Khaṣīf says all creatures. Fire serves light, warmth, cooking and baking; Ibn Kathīr prefers this broader account for rich and poor, residents and nomads, and says God embedded fire in stones and pure iron so travelers could carry tools to kindle it. Al-Mahdawī says every class needs fire. Al-Ālūsī's general 'people in need' account overlaps this universal benefit."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p3", "position": "Hungry people whose stomachs are empty.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd invokes aqwaytu, 'I have eaten nothing'; al-Qurṭubī adds sleeping in qiwāʾ or qafr without a meal and an unnamed poet who prefers hunger to being called mean. The hungry cook food over fire. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak; Abū Ḥayyān calls it very weak; al-Ālūsī objects that hunger can be relieved without cooked food. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuran Yolu combine hunger with desert travel, deriving both from emptiness."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p4", "position": "The poor or those lacking provisions, wealth, or fire-starting supplies.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda derives it from provisions running out and from an empty house; Ibn ʿĪsā says weakness and poverty. Al-Rabīʿ and al-Suddī say destitute people kindle fire to bake, roast game, or, in al-Qurṭubī's variant, lack fire-starting sticks; al-ʿAwfī also transmits the interpretation from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Māwardī cites al-Nābigha on travelers left with a fire drill and kindling. Al-Ālūsī says poor people need warmth and light; Elmalılı adds gathering and selling wood. Ibn Qutayba rejects lack of provisions as the defining sense because a provisioned traveler needs fire more."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p5", "position": "Both poor and wealthy people, since muqwī has opposite senses.", "reasons": "Quṭrub explains poverty as lack of property, wealth as strong animals or abundant possessions; al-Ṭībī and al-Ṭabarsī report the same opposition, linking wealth with power to get one's desires. Al-Ṭabarī notes that outside this context muqwī can mean a strong-horse owner or rich person; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī also record the strong sense. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects deriving the desert sense from the distinct strong-mount verb, likening it to atraba; al-Ālūsī questions the opposites account and favors 'in need.'"}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p6", "position": "One who kindles, strengthens, and feeds the fire.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī bases this sense on the person adding fuel to the fire."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p7", "position": "Anyone in need of fire.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers this sense as more plausible than the opposites account, because everyone who enjoys fire needs it."}, {"id": "56:73/q05/p8", "position": "People lost in a desolate place, including the lonely and spiritually hungry.", "reasons": "Asad derives a literal desolate or hungry sense from qawiya/qawāʾ/qiwa, then renders it tropically for lonely, unfortunate and confused people seeking human warmth and spiritual light. He rejects restriction to desert wayfarers."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q06", "question": "Why are desert travelers or dwellers singled out as fire’s beneficiaries?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q06/p1", "position": "They have an especially strong practical need for fire.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qushayrī, al-Ālūsī, Bursawī and Elmalılı cite night protection from predators and multiple needs; al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī add guiding lost people. Bursawī lists warmth, drying clothes and cooking, and says settled neighbors can obtain fire without kindling; al-Ālūsī likewise contrasts nearby residents or travelers. Ibn Qutayba argues a supplied traveler has greater need than one without provisions. Ibn Kathīr says travelers are named despite universal use; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds lighting and warming camps, guiding night travelers, and cooking at home or on journeys."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q07", "question": "What inward senses are given to the fire, its reminder, and its provision?", "turns_on": "These readings transfer the verse's fire, warning, provision, or desolation to spiritual experience.", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q07/p1", "position": "It warns the pious and conveys the gnostic saints.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports Jaʿfar's explanation."}, {"id": "56:73/q07/p2", "position": "It recalls the primordial covenant and provisions spiritual wayfarers lacking knowledge and practice.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī pairs these two inward senses."}, {"id": "56:73/q07/p3", "position": "The inward fire is love, and its provision is spiritual food for ascetic lovers.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Manṣūr calls the fire love kindled in a sincere lover's heart, its tree eternal divine care; without that care one would not know Book or faith. Bursawī describes lovers abstaining from food and drink; he cites Sahl al-Tustarī fasting thirty days, Abū ʿAqīl eating nothing for two years in Mecca, other ascetics, and a report of Idrīs ascending to the fourth heaven or sphere of the Sun after sixteen years without sleep, food or marriage."}, {"id": "56:73/q07/p4", "position": "Desolate hunger also describes longing for human warmth and spiritual light.", "reasons": "Asad applies the literal desert and hunger wording to lonely, unfortunate and confused people."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q08", "question": "Why is the afterlife reminder placed before worldly use?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q08/p1", "position": "The afterlife benefit is more important and deserves priority.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls it fuller and more worthy of attention; Bursawī and al-Ālūsī likewise read the order as directing attention to it."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q09", "question": "What is reported about earthly fire compared with Hellfire?", "turns_on": "The reports measure different qualities: the familiar one-seventieth heat comparison and a separate darkness comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q09/p1", "position": "Earthly fire is one part in seventy of Hellfire.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports Qatāda and the Prophet; al-Kashshāf states no grading. Al-Qurṭubī reports that when Companions said earthly fire sufficed, the Prophet said Hell has sixty-nine further parts, each as hot. Ibn Kathīr labels Qatāda's route mursal; he also cites Aḥmad from Abū Hurayra, and Bukhārī and Muslim for the sixty-nine further parts, with Muslim's each-part wording. Al-Ālūsī cites the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections. The Study Quran and Bursawī repeat the ratio. In some versions God struck or cooled earthly fire twice with water so people could approach and use it; Ibn Kathīr's Aḥmad route says twice by the sea."}, {"id": "56:73/q09/p2", "position": "Hellfire is seventy times darker than earthly fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites al-Ṭabarānī from Abū Hurayra; al-Ḍiyāʾ al-Maqdisī notes Ibn Muṣʿab transmitted it from Mālik without raising it to the Prophet and considers it to meet sound-hadith conditions."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q10", "question": "What other reports illustrate the severity of Hellfire?", "turns_on": "The two narrations illustrate severity in different ways.", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q10/p1", "position": "Michael has not laughed since the Fire was created.", "reasons": "Bursawī relays the Prophet asking Gabriel why Michael never smiles and Gabriel's answer."}, {"id": "56:73/q10/p2", "position": "The least punished inhabitant of Hell wears sandals that boil his brain.", "reasons": "Bursawī transmits Anas; the report underlines Hell's excess over worldly fire, and the narrator prays for protection."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q11", "question": "What is reported about sharing the fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q11/p1", "position": "Fire is a shared resource and may not be withheld.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr gives a Prophetic report through a man of the Muhājirūn of Qarn that Muslims share fire, pasture and water, transmitted by Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd. Abū Hurayra's version forbids withholding the three; Ibn Mājah transmits it with a good chain. Ibn ʿAbbās's version adds a ban on charging, but its chain has the weak ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kharrāsh ibn Ḥawshab."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q12", "question": "How does this fire connect with the preceding signs of provision?", "turns_on": "Al-Ālūsī disputes the culinary sequence and instead explains the order by the relative urgency and generality of water.", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q12/p1", "position": "The passage moves from creation to grain, water, then fire needed to bake food.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī relates human creation, grain, water used with food and cooking fire to 56:58, 63, 68 and 71; these sustain bodily

Al-Ālūsī reports the same proposed order with references to 56:58, 64 and 69, but finds the rationale unconvincing."}, {"id": "56:73/q12/p2", "position": "Water comes before fire because its need and benefit are more widespread and urgent.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this explanation of the order."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q13", "question": "Why does the passage describe fire without threatening its removal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q13/p1", "position": "People can survive without fire, whereas food and water are indispensable.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts this with the earlier food and water passages."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q14", "question": "What is reported about responding to the preceding rhetorical questions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q14/p1", "position": "ʿAlī answered them with 'Rather, You, Lord,' but scholars dispute doing so during prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports Ḥujr al-Marwazī hearing ʿAlī respond three times after each question on procreation, crops, water and fire (56:58, 64, 69, 72); he notes disagreement over whether the answer is recommended in ritual prayer."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q15", "question": "How does fire from wood answer mockery of Hell’s tree?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q15/p1", "position": "God’s joining fire and tree in this world shows He can create Zaqqūm in Hell.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī points to worldly markh and ʿafār as the analogy answering Quraysh's mockery of 17:60 and relates it to 56:52–53."}]}
{"id": "56:73/q16", "question": "What theological response does God’s creation of fire demand?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:73/q16/p1", "position": "People should thank God and acknowledge His power to resurrect.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reasons that God is the inventor and creator, so denial of resurrection is unfitting."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q01", "question": "What does the command to glorify involve?", "turns_on": "Whether tasbih is primarily repudiation of false claims, remembrance or spoken formula, prayer, inward realization, public proclamation, or reverence for the divine name; several sources allow more than one act.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q01/p1", "position": "Declare God transcendent above false descriptions, partners, imperfection, and denial of His power to resurrect.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Basit and Wahidi-Wajiz specify people's and polytheists' claims; Ibn Atiyya specifies the unbelievers' treatment of God's exalted names. Tabrisi purifies God of unfit descriptions; al-Zajjaj, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, connects this to proofs of unity, power, and favor. Qurtubi identifies alleged partners and inability to resurrect. Nasafi says what does not befit Him; Biqai especially names denial of resurrection. Tabatabai specifies shirk and denial of recompense. Elmalili includes partners and imperfection. Study Quran defines tasbih as declaring transcendence beyond everything and says deficiencies perceived in God's works cannot be attributed to Him. Muqatil includes remembrance of divine oneness."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p2", "position": "Remember and invoke God by His name, including His beautiful names.", "reasons": "Nahhas mentions remembrance and the beautiful names; Muqatil makes that remembrance one of unity. Ibn Jarir, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, says to remember and name the Lord. Kashshaf and Baydawi allow 'name' to mean remembrance; Nasafi and Study Quran also give invocation by name. Alusi prefers the ordinary meaning of mentioning the Lord or His name. Study Quran's Aj says God's glory exceeds anything anyone can say of it."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p3", "position": "Utter a formula of praise, especially 'subḥān Allāh' or 'subḥāna rabbī al-ʿaẓīm.'", "reasons": "Kashshaf gives subḥān Allāh; Razi allows it or equivalent words. Tabrisi and Nasafi give subḥāna rabbī al-ʿaẓīm; Tabrisi relates it to the Prophet's instruction for bowing. Elmalili gives the latter formula alongside prayer. Baydawi permits uttering the name."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p4", "position": "Pray in the Lord's name, beginning prayer with the takbīr.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, gives the prayer and its opening takbīr; Elmalili also allows prayer as the response."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p5", "position": "Realize divine unity inwardly through belief, deep reflection, knowledge, and protection of faith from doubt.", "reasons": "Qushayri describes thinking deeply and using the strength of unity to find knowledge and guard faith. Razi includes inward conviction that God is one without partner and can resurrect; he says true unity excludes body, accident, location, and being in, on, or from anything, while power entails knowledge, will, life, and other attributes, with reference to al-Ikhlas (112:1)."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p6", "position": "Name and describe God aloud among one's people, continuing to preach despite their refusal.", "reasons": "Razi says purely inward tasbih would not communicate the proclamation; the Lord is named and described publicly."}, {"id": "56:74/q01/p7", "position": "Honor and protect God's own name and its words from disrespect.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says to clear God's exalted names of unbelievers' claims. Alusi argues literally that, if God's essence and attributes are free from defects, the words used for them deserve freedom from disrespect even more, comparing 87:1. Biqai says mentioning the name most firmly honors the One named."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q02", "question": "How does 'by the name of your Lord' work?", "turns_on": "Whether bāʾ is instrumental, associative, transitive, introductory, additional, or expresses seeking aid, and whether 'name' means the uttered name, remembrance, the divine essence, or attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q02/p1", "position": "The bāʾ marks means or accompaniment: glorify by naming, mentioning, or remembering the Lord.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Baydawi allow name to mean remembrance. Razi explains that the real object is the Lord through the name, so the relation permits a preposition. Bursevi treats the glorifying verb as intransitive and the bāʾ as means or accompaniment. Alusi supplies 'by mentioning' or treats 'name' figuratively as mention; he accepts means or accompaniment but rejects Abu Hayyan's apparent transitive analysis. Tabatabai says naming is mentioning and the bāʾ can mean use or association. Wāsiṭī, reported by Sulami, says a thing's name is the thing itself."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p2", "position": "The bāʾ or 'name' is additional, giving the direct sense 'glorify your Lord.'", "reasons": "An unnamed view reported by Ibn al-Jawzi makes bāʾ extra and name stand for the divine essence. Razi reports the common parsing that makes 'name' extra, while saying its mention still heightens reverence because the truly exalted are named by greatness. Alusi objects that a symbolic direct-Lord interpretation needs omission or an extra bāʾ and conflicts with apparent wording."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p3", "position": "Sanctify the Lord's name itself, thereby sanctifying the Lord.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reports a transitive analysis: purify the name from association and from denial of resurrection and recompense. Alusi defends literal reverence for the words used of God because His essence and attributes are free from defects; he objects to readings that require dropping the bāʾ or treating it as extra. Ibn Atiyya speaks of clearing His exalted names from unbelievers' claims."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p4", "position": "Begin the glorification with the Lord's name.", "reasons": "Kashshaf offers beginning by uttering the name; Razi says this leaves bāʾ meaningful. Alusi reports the intransitive 'begin glorifying' construction but discusses its temporal force separately."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p5", "position": "Reserve the divine name for God alone rather than giving it to idols.", "reasons": "Razi says idolaters concede God created all things yet name idols gods, so the meaningful bāʾ prohibits that designation and admonishes any hearer. Alusi reports a related view directed to an idolater who admits God created them and the heavens and earth; Alusi says this particularized address is unnecessary."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p6", "position": "The bāʾ expresses seeking the Lord's help while glorifying Him.", "reasons": "Islahi says the Prophet seeks aid against the circumstances posed by stubborn rejecters."}, {"id": "56:74/q02/p7", "position": "The name signifies God's noble attributes as the means of knowing and relating to Him.", "reasons": "Islahi says these attributes source true knowledge and deeds. Nahhas refers to God's beautiful names in the act of remembrance."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q03", "question": "Why is the alif of 'ism' written here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q03/p1", "position": "The alif is retained because this spelling occurs less often than the basmala.", "reasons": "Biqai contrasts the frequent basmala, whose repeated use encourages an abbreviated spelling."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q04", "question": "What does 'the Great' describe?", "turns_on": "Whether al-ʿaẓīm is syntactically attached to the Lord or His name; Ibn Ashur supplies a metaphorical account of the latter, and Kuranyolu prefers the former.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q04/p1", "position": "It modifies 'Lord': the Lord is Great.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Alusi, Tabatabai, Study Quran citing Bḍ, and Ibn Ashur all allow this attachment. Ibn Ashur says every divine perfection is established. Kuranyolu prefers it as the usual attachment and translates 'the name of your mighty Lord.'"}, {"id": "56:74/q04/p2", "position": "It modifies 'name': the name is Great.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Alusi, Tabatabai, Study Quran citing Bḍ, and Kuranyolu allow this attachment. Ibn Ashur says greatness of the name is a common metaphor, nearly literal, arising from its blessing and the greatness of the One named. Kuranyolu gives the alternative wording 'glorify your Lor
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

d by His mighty name.'"}]}
{"id": "56:74/q05", "question": "What greatness is conveyed by 'the Great'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q05/p1", "position": "God's greatness encompasses majesty and every perfection while transcending defect and perception.", "reasons": "Muqatil says He is the greatest. Biqai says His majesty fills the cosmos, He transcends every defect and lacks no perfection. Razi says perceptible greatness suggests nearness to all, yet God transcends perception and His positive attributes exceed knowledge; Ibn Ashur says every divine perfection is established. Wāsiṭī says He is the Great."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q06", "question": "How does 'the Great' compare with 'the Most High' in 87:1?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q06/p1", "position": "'The Most High' more directly expresses transcendence and is the more apt epithet, while 'the Great' combines affirmation and negation.", "reasons": "Razi compares the epithets with 87:1: perceptible greatness suggests nearness, absolute elevation remoteness, though God transcends perception and His positive attributes outrun knowledge. He explicitly prefers al-Aʿlā as more apt usage."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q07", "question": "Who is addressed by the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the second-person address remains the Prophet's, extends generally to hearers, or identifies a particular idolater; Alusi questions the need for particularization.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q07/p1", "position": "The Prophet is addressed, with his response standing against the deniers.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it a command to the Prophet after the signs. Razi describes his task after deniers reject creation and provision proofs. Tabrisi, Tabatabai, Islahi, and Ibn Ashur explicitly identify the Messenger or Prophet; Ibn Ashur calls the worship a fresh recollection of majesty and gratitude. Biqai says the Lord specially benefited the Prophet by supreme clarification."}, {"id": "56:74/q07/p2", "position": "The command addresses any hearer, including idolaters who acknowledge God as Creator.", "reasons": "Razi makes the ban on assigning the divine name to idols an admonition to any hearer. Alusi reports a proposed particular idolater but says it can be a generic preacher's 'O poor man'; a general address is possible and the particularization is not required. Study Quran treats the verse as one of many commands to human beings to glorify God."}, {"id": "56:74/q07/p3", "position": "A particular idolater is addressed to acknowledge that no other deity shares God's name.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this view because idolaters admit that God created them and the heavens and earth. He objects that the particular addressee is unnecessary and could be understood generically."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q08", "question": "What is the force of commanding glorification when the Prophet already does it?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative introduces an act, renews an already continuous act, or urges the Prophet to persevere publicly; al-Tibi disputes making 'begin' mean 'continue'.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q08/p1", "position": "The command calls for renewed, distinct glorification after fresh reflection on the signs.", "reasons": "Al-Tibi objects to explaining 'begin' as 'continue' and prefers renewal. Ibn Ashur says the Messenger always glorifies God, yet each renewed reflection produces a distinct worship state with its own merits and greater reward; the command is a fresh recollection of majesty and gratitude."}, {"id": "56:74/q08/p2", "position": "The command says to begin glorification, effectively to continue it since the Prophet never neglected it.", "reasons": "Alusi reports an intransitive construal of a transitive verb; al-Tibi objects that taking 'beginning' as continuing reverses the force of the wording."}, {"id": "56:74/q08/p3", "position": "The Prophet should hold his stance and keep glorifying despite stubborn rejection.", "reasons": "Islahi says the arguments support him against the rejecters; Razi says he must perfect knowledge and service and continue naming God publicly even when his people refuse."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q09", "question": "Why does the command follow the preceding signs?", "turns_on": "The cited purposes are inference and gratitude from the signs, repudiation of deniers, possible astonishment at ingratitude, or a transition through recitation to the following oath; Alusi disputes the astonishment reading.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q09/p1", "position": "The signs of creation, provision, divine power, and favor call for glorification and gratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj in Ibn al-Jawzi ties it to proof of unity, power, and favor; Kashshaf and Baydawi name power and blessings. Tabrisi invokes signs of oneness and favors; Qushayri and Biqai say they prepare inference. Biqai adds wonder and magnification; Alusi says the command follows marvelous works and gifts and reports gratitude as praise of the true Benefactor. Bursevi thanks God despite deniers. Ibn Ashur finds fresh majesty and gratitude after resurrection examples and blessings. Tabatabai reads fa as making glorification follow the proof. Study Quran says God transcends the listed works and their perceived deficiencies in 56:58–73."}, {"id": "56:74/q09/p2", "position": "The command rejects deniers' claims about God's oneness, resurrection, and favors after the proofs establish them.", "reasons": "Wahidi-Wajiz and Ibn Atiyya name polytheists or unbelievers. Kashshaf and Baydawi contrast denial with the signs. Qurtubi names partners and alleged incapacity to resurrect; Biqai especially opposes resurrection denial. Razi links the deniers' rejection to perfecting knowledge and service, citing 20:130. Alusi reports denials of unity and gifts; Tabatabai says the command turns from uncomprehending deniers after signs of lordship; Islahi says self-evident arguments about Judgment sustain the Prophet despite Quraysh's resistance."}, {"id": "56:74/q09/p3", "position": "The response also expresses amazement at the disbelievers' ingratitude.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, and Biqai allow this purpose. Alusi reports it but objects that taking subḥān metaphorically as astonishment is distant and prefers repudiation or gratitude."}, {"id": "56:74/q09/p4", "position": "The verse directs recitation of the Qur'an or this sūra, preparing the following oath.", "reasons": "Al-Kashf, reported by Alusi, says recitation establishes resurrection, recompense, and ranks before the oath at 56:75."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q10", "question": "How do the preceding examples support the command?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize either the evidential force of creation and livelihood for resurrection and lordship, or a classification of opposing conditions, elements, and life-sustaining qualities.", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q10/p1", "position": "The enumerated signs supply grounds for inference about God and resurrection.", "reasons": "Qushayri says their enumeration prepares reflection; Biqai transmits this and a report, without authority or grading, that an hour's reflection is better than sixty years' worship. Ibn Kathir notes sweet water could have become salty and fire benefits worldly life while warning of the Hereafter. Abu Hayyan in Biqai groups creation with food, drink, and fire, and treats fire's transformation as evidence of resurrection. Tabatabai names crops, water, and fire as necessities showing lordship as governance rooted in ownership after creation and allotted death. Islahi sees self-evident proofs of Judgment, insisting the world was not made merely for luxury or sport and a day must reward gratitude and punish ingratitude."}, {"id": "56:74/q10/p2", "position": "The examples are organized around opposing conditions and the elements and qualities that sustain life.", "reasons": "Biqai reports Razi's richest opposing pair as becoming rich and poor. He reports Ibn Barjan's linkage of water and earth with creation of the elements, and air and fire with temperaments and qualities; Ibn Barjan says the sun's heat, as hellfire, produces gardens, fruit, crops, and livelihoods. Abu Hayyan groups the examples as creation and necessities of livelihood."}]}
{"id": "56:74/q11", "question": "What was the Prophet's instruction when this verse was revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "56:74/q11/p1", "position": "He told worshippers to say its glorification during bowing.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Nasafi report the instruction at revelation; Tabrisi also identifies the formula as 'Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty.'"}]}

{"id": "58:6/q02", "question": "What governs the accusative yawm?", "turns_on": "Which preceding expression or supplied verb supplies the time phrase's syntactic governor; the later aḥṣāhu and al-kāfirīn attachments draw express criticism.", "positions": [{"id": "58:6/q02/p1", "position": "The preceding humiliating punishment, or its qualifying word or implied predicate, governs it.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas attach it to the punishment of 58:5; Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi specify mahīn, while Ibn 'Ashur allows either mahīn or an implied predicate of the unbelievers' punishment. {"id": "58:6/q03", "question": "Is yawm inflected or built here?", "turns_on": "Whether a time noun before a future verb can be built, as the Kufans infer from its meaning of idhā, or must remain inflected under the Basran restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "58:6/q03/p1", "position": "It is an inflected accusative governed by the preceding punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says Basran grammarians reject building yawm before a future verb; they permit that only before a past verb or an indeclinable form."}, {"id": "58:6/q03/p2", "position": "It is built because it has the sense of idhā.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas reports this as the Kufan analysis."}]}

{"id": "58:6/q07", "question": "What does God's informing them of their deeds do?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording foregrounds factual disclosure and proof, public disgrace, manifested deed-forms, or the consequences of the deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "58:6/q07/p1", "position": "He tells them all their deeds, including hidden acts, to establish the proof against them.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and al-Wahidi stress their recognition of binding proof. {"id": "58:6/q20", "question": "What aims are ascribed to narratives about the Israelites?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "58:6/q20/p1", "position": "They prove prophethood, recall favors, explain rejection of prophets, and warn later hearers of analogous punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Qaffal, reported by al-Burhan, says knowledge available only by revelation proves Muhammad's prophethood; the accounts recall favors to Israel, show their ancestors' rejection and foreshadow descendants' treatment of Muhammad, and warn contemporaries by earlier punishments."}]}
